content.title: About
content.content: Raw asparagus consists of the young shoots of Asparagus officinalis, cultivated in temperate climates. It has a delicate, slightly nutty flavor and a crisp texture. Asparagus can be eaten raw in salads or briefly cooked for a tender bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Asparagus is one of the oldest cultivated vegetables, with a history of over 2,000 years.
In ancient Roman medicine it was used as a diuretic and liver tonic.
Fresh asparagus season runs from early spring to early summer.
There are several varieties: green, white (grown in darkness), and purple.
Raw asparagus is a rich source of folate, important for cell division.

items.title: Rich in folate
items.content: Folate supports DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Raw asparagus provides very few calories, making it ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: It supplies vitamin C, vitamin E and glutathione, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium and dietary fiber help maintain normal blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: While not a major protein source, asparagus contributes to daily protein intake.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to asparagus.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large amounts of raw asparagus can cause gas and discomfort due to its fiber content.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Asparagus contains oxalates, which in excess may contribute to kidney stone formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice raw asparagus thinly and add to salads, smoothies, or marinate it. It can also be briefly blanched in boiling water for a softer texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store asparagus in the refrigerator wrapped in a slightly damp towel and placed in a plastic bag. Use within 3–5 days. Discard if yellow spots or off‑odors develop.

content.title: About
content.content: Molasses cookie is a soft, aromatic biscuit made from wheat flour, butter, sugar and molasses. Molasses gives the cookie its dark color and a rich caramel‑to‑honey flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Molasses is a by‑product of sugar production from cane or beet and is rich in minerals and B‑vitamins.
The dark hue of the cookie comes from the high melasse content, which contains iron, calcium and magnesium.
Traditionally these cookies are made in colder regions where molasses was used as a natural sweetener during winter.
Molasses cookies are often served with tea or coffee, as their sweetness pairs well with bitter drinks.
In some countries molasses is considered a healthier alternative to refined sugar because of its lower glycemic index.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Molasses provides iron, calcium, magnesium and potassium, supporting blood, bone and muscle function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: The dark color indicates the presence of polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact
items.content: Molasses has a lower glycemic index than regular sugar, which may reduce sharp blood‑glucose spikes.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The cookie offers a quick source of energy thanks to its blend of carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A small amount of dietary fiber in the cookie aids normal digestive function.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Despite a lower glycemic index, molasses still contains a significant amount of sugar, so consumption should be moderate.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: The cookie contains gluten, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Molasses cookies are relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised, especially for weight management.

items.title: Potential heavy‑metal traces
items.content: Some batches of molasses may contain trace amounts of lead or cadmium; choose reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Molasses cookies can be enjoyed as a snack, added to yogurt, ice cream, or used in dessert recipes. They pair well with nuts, dried fruit, and cream cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent softening from moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Shark is a marine predatory fish found in oceans worldwide. Shark meat is valued for its firm texture, mild flavor, and high protein content. It is commonly used in sushi, grilling, soups, and stews.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: There are over 500 shark species, ranging from tiny dwarf lanternsharks to massive whale sharks.
Most sharks have multiple rows of teeth that are continuously replaced throughout their lives.
Some shark species can detect the electric fields generated by the movement of their prey.
Shark meat contains low to moderate levels of mercury, so moderate consumption is advised.
In several cultures, shark meat is considered a delicacy and featured in traditional dishes.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Shark meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many other seafoods, shark has relatively low saturated fat content.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: It contains EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Shark meat supplies B12, B6, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It is a source of selenium, zinc, and iron, nutrients that aid immunity and blood formation.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Meat from large predatory sharks may contain higher mercury levels; pregnant women and children should limit intake.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including shark.

items.title: Texture
items.content: If not cooked properly, shark meat can be tough, increasing the risk of choking or esophageal injury.

items.title: Parasites
items.content: Like other fish, shark can harbor parasites; it should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Shark meat can be grilled, baked, stewed, or used in sushi and sashimi after proper freezing. Marinating in lemon juice or vinegar before cooking helps tenderize the flesh.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh shark in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C for no more than 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw completely in the refrigerator before use.

meat-loaf-made-with-beef-veal-and-pork.title: Meat loaf made with beef, veal and pork

content.title: About
content.content: Meat loaf made with beef, veal and pork is a baked dish composed of ground meats, eggs, breadcrumbs and seasonings. It is traditionally formed into a solid loaf, sliced, and often served with sauce or a side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the 19th‑century United States as a way to use leftover meat.
Combining beef, veal and pork provides a balance of flavor and texture: beef adds richness, veal adds tenderness, pork adds juiciness.
Milk or cream is often added to keep the loaf moist.
Meat loaf is frequently served cold as a sandwich filling.
Regional variations may include vegetables such as onion, carrot or celery.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef and veal contain heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support immune function and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full for longer.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Pork contributes saturated fat, which should be limited for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt or soy sauce can raise sodium levels, a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor pathogens; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C (160 °F).

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some recipes include dairy or gluten, which can trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the loaf and serve hot or cold. It pairs well with mustard, tomato sauce, horseradish, or vegetable sides. Ideal for sandwiches, salads and snack platters.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 4 days. For longer storage, freeze in sealed bags for up to 3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 71 °C before eating.

tuna-salad-made-with-light-creamy-dressi.title: Tuna Salad with Light Creamy Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna salad with light creamy dressing is a ready‑to‑eat mix of premium tuna, fresh vegetables and a gentle yogurt‑based sauce with a hint of light cheese. It offers a mild flavor, subtle tang and a smooth texture, making it a convenient snack or light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the richest sources of omega‑3 fatty acids, beneficial for heart and brain health.
The light creamy dressing often includes lemon juice, which keeps the flavor bright.
Athletes frequently include this salad in their diet because of its high protein and low calorie profile.
Canned tuna used in the salad is typically flash‑cooked, preserving most nutrients.
In several countries the tuna salad is a classic picnic dish.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support cardiovascular health and reduce inflammatory processes.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Tuna provides a complete set of essential amino acids for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The light dressing makes the dish less calorie‑dense than traditional mayonnaise‑based salads.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna supplies vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The salad contains selenium and magnesium, which aid antioxidant protection and normal muscle function.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tuna.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned tuna often contains added salt, so people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Mercury exposure
items.content: Tuna can contain trace amounts of mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Lactose in dressing
items.content: If the sauce uses dairy cheese, those with lactose intolerance should choose a lactose‑free alternative.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The salad is ready to eat straight from the package. It can be added to sandwiches, wrapped in flatbread, served with whole‑grain crackers, or used as a filling for vegetable rolls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0 °C‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3‑4 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.
